note: The plain-English Q&A. Each question sets levers or fields on the nodes the sentence created. 'target' is a node type, 'subjects' (people who aren't staff), or 'flow' (asked once; answers set fields on the flow itself with 'flow'). A question with several matching nodes is asked once per node; {title} is the node's name. 'type' is 'single' (pick one answer) or 'checklist' (tick any that are true; each item has 'on' and 'off' settings). 'show_when' hides a question or item unless it's true. 'skip_when' skips a question we already know the answer to (from the product directory or a company card). The interview also skips any question where no answer would change the result, and records it as assumed, not asked.

questions.ask: Which of these are true about {title}?
questions.why: Each one changes how sensitive the data is, or what people need to be told. Tick any that apply; leave the rest.

items.label: It says how someone is doing
items.hint: Marks, attendance, behaviour, feedback, support notes

items.label: It could mention health, SEND, religion, ethnicity, sexuality or crime
items.hint: The most sensitive kind of data. It stays in organisation systems or an approved route, and needs an extra legal condition.

items.label: It's in people's own words, written or spoken
items.hint: Essays, comments boxes, recordings. Anything could be in there.

items.label: We already have it, but got it for a different reason
items.hint: Attendance you keep anyway, now used to predict who might drop out

items.label: We'd be collecting it new
items.hint: A new form, a new login, a new survey

items.label: Under 18s will use the tool themselves
items.hint: A revision app students log into. The ICO's Children's code then applies.

questions.ask: Once in the tool, will {title} have people's names on?
questions.why: Swapping names for a code is often the single easiest way to make an idea simpler to approve.
questions.example: A candidate number instead of a name, with the list kept inside the organisation.

answers.label: A code we can look up

questions.ask: What's the legal reason you're allowed to use {title}?
questions.why: Every use of personal data needs a lawful basis. Consent sounds safest but often isn't valid for students or staff, because they can't freely say no to the organisation.
questions.example: Teaching, marking and supporting students are part of a school or college's job, so 'public task' usually fits.

answers.label: It's part of our job (public task)
It's needed for a contract with them

questions.ask: Which of these are true about {title}?
questions.why: These are the warning signs the ICO looks for. Ticking one doesn't mean no; it means it needs a closer look.

items.label: It gives someone a mark, grade, score or prediction
items.hint: A suggested grade, a risk score, a 'likely to pass' flag

items.label: Things can happen to a person without a human checking first
items.hint: An automatic fail, an automatic referral

items.label: It could stop someone getting something
items.hint: Blocking enrolment, refusing an extension, removing access

items.label: It covers everyone, or over a thousand people
items.hint: Every student in the college, not one class

items.label: It keeps running, not a one-off
items.hint: Weekly checks rather than one survey

items.label: It tracks what individuals do, when or where
items.hint: Login times per student, what they click, where they are

questions.ask: Have the people it's about been told their data is used like this?
questions.why: People have a right to know. Usually that's a line in the privacy notice.
questions.example: A sentence in the student privacy notice about using AI to help with marking.

answers.label: Yes, it's in our privacy notice

questions.why: The same product is a different thing on each plan. Free and personal plans usually train on what you type and come with no contract; business plans don't train and include a data protection agreement.
questions.example: Free ChatGPT on personal logins, versus ChatGPT Business paid for by the organisation.

questions.ask: Two honest checks. Are either of these true?
questions.why: These are the ones people skip. If either is true, the idea needs changing before anything else, so it's better to know now.

items.label: We could get the same result with less data, or without names
items.hint: If a gentler design does the job, the law expects you to use it.

items.label: We couldn't show, delete or explain someone's data if they asked
items.hint: People have these rights whatever the tool.

questions.ask: What will the AI in {title} actually do?
questions.why: Your organisation sets a minimum level of checking for each kind of AI use. The closer it gets to a final decision, the more checking.
questions.example: Drafting a lesson plan is very different from suggesting a grade.

answers.label: Help with general work, nothing about people
Work with things people can be identified from

questions.ask: Will {title} sign up to our terms: a data protection agreement, using data only as we say?
questions.why: A company that handles your data has to be bound by contract. If they won't sign, that's a firm no, whatever else is true.
questions.example: Microsoft's Data Protection Addendum covers Microsoft 365 and Copilot.

answers.label: Yes, it's signed or on offer

questions.ask: Could {title} use what you put in to train its AI?
questions.why: If they train on it, people's data leaves your control for good. Free and consumer versions often do.
questions.example: Consumer chatbots often train on chats unless you opt out; business versions usually don't.

answers.label: No, the contract rules it out

questions.ask: Who will own this and decide whether the risk is worth it?
questions.why: Someone with the authority to change the project has to accept any risk that's left, in writing. The DPO gives advice; they don't approve. A risk nobody owns is the one that goes wrong quietly.
questions.example: A deputy principal, or the head of the department running it. A role, not a name.

answers.label: The head of the department running it
